lockedMove.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
lockedMove.proposition: Even an exhaustive set of hypotheses does not warrant believing the member assigned the largest probability when none has sufficient evidential support; the rational conclusion may remain unknown.

components.text: Whether the largest-probability member of an exhaustive hypothesis set must be believed when its evidential support remains insufficient.
Whether a qualitative probability framework permits rational suspension when data do not warrant reliable assignments or a sufficiently probable conclusion.

response.rationale: The reply identifies why exhaustiveness alone fails and states the consequence that rational judgment may remain unknown when no hypothesis clears sufficient support.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes logical exhaustiveness, relative ranking, and sufficient warrant, with an explicit threshold-style qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is properly permissive: uncertainty may be rational when evidence is insufficient, rather than uncertainty being mandatory in every exhaustive comparison.

charity.alternative: A probability distribution can rationally rank exhaustive hypotheses even when no member exceeds one-half, and action may favor the largest member.
charity.decisiveQualification: Ranking or action preference does not necessarily warrant belief that the largest member occurred, especially when assignments are poorly grounded.

lockedMove.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that exhaustive options can coexist with insufficient data and that the rational conclusion may therefore be that the event is unknown.

immutablePublicationFields.words: An exhaustive hypothesis set does not require belief in its largest member when probability assignments remain poorly grounded or every option lacks sufficient evidential support.
